terms.definition: The words of the Act are given their plain, ordinary meaning, even if the result is absurd.
terms.examiner: Whiteley v Chappell, LNER v Berriman, Fisher v Bell. It respects parliamentary sovereignty but can produce unjust results: have one case for each side.

terms.definition: A modification of the literal rule: where the literal meaning would give an absurd result, the court may avoid it.
terms.examiner: Narrow approach: choose between possible meanings of a word (Allen, Adler v George). Wider approach: modify the words to avoid a repugnant result (Re Sigsworth).

terms.definition: The court looks at the gap or "mischief" in the law that the Act was passed to remedy, and interprets the Act so as to remedy it.
terms.examiner: Heydon's Case (1584) sets out the four questions. Smith v Hughes and Royal College of Nursing v DHSS are the usual examples.

terms.definition: The court looks for the purpose of Parliament in passing the Act and interprets the words to give effect to that purpose.
terms.examiner: R v Registrar-General ex parte Smith; R (Quintavalle) v Secretary of State for Health. It goes further than the mischief rule: the court is not limited to the gap in the old law.

terms.definition: Matters within the Act itself that help to make its meaning clear.
terms.examiner: The long and short title, the preamble, headings, interpretation sections and schedules.

terms.definition: Matters outside the Act that the court may use to help interpret it.
terms.examiner: Dictionaries of the time, the Interpretation Act 1978, Law Commission reports, explanatory notes, and Hansard under the conditions in Pepper v Hart (1993).

terms.definition: So far as it is possible to do so, legislation must be read and given effect in a way that is compatible with Convention rights.
terms.examiner: Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza is the standard example of the courts reading words into a statute to make it compatible.
